title: The shoemaker of Benares
hookLine: Ravidas, a leather-worker whose family were counted low, sings that the leading Brahmins now bow to him (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)

lines: HE SAYS WHERE HE CAME FROM.
cards: Some people learn to hide where they come from. They soften the accent, skip the hometown, let others guess. Ravidas did the opposite.

Tradition says he worked leather in Benares, the holy city on the Ganges, at a bench where shoes were cut and stitched and mended. Some people of his day wouldn't touch a leather-worker, or drink from the same cup.
Yet his hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one of them he says, without any shame, exactly where he came from.

teach.b: The hymn is in Raag Malar, on Ang 1293. Its turn, in paraphrase: my people work in leather, and every day they carry dead cattle around Benares.
Now the leading Brahmins bow down before me, for I, Ravidas your servant, have taken shelter in your Name. Hear the order of those lines. He starts with the hardest thing to say.
Not a soft word for his trade, but the work itself: hauling dead cattle through the lanes of a holy city. Then the reversal. The very people at the top of that world now bow to him.
And notice what he credits. Not his talent, not his luck. The Name.
He has taken shelter there, and that shelter changed how he is seen. The second turn: Ravidas doesn't try to escape his family.
He names them first, before he names himself, and keeps them in the song, dead cattle and all. The third turn is the Sikh book. The Granth keeps Ravidas's hymns inside the ragas, under his own name.
In gurdwaras his words are sung as gurbani, and Sikhs bow to the book that holds them.
A leather-worker's song stands in the same place as a Guru's. He didn't trade his family's name for a grander one. He sang with it.

how: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as gurbani, and Sikhs and Ravidassia communities honor him as a saint whose life challenged caste.

o: a learned Brahmin of Benares who bowed to the poor
a shoemaker's tool for stitching leather by hand

games.q: you're Ravidas, singing about your life. how do you describe your family?
o: skip it and sing only of the Lord.
name their work plainly: they carry dead cattle around Benares.
games.why: he names it plainly, then sings that the leading Brahmins now bow before him.

practice: Take any pair of shoes into your lap with a cloth, a little polish, or a damp rag, and work slowly around the toe, along the seams, down to the heel, feeling the leather or canvas under your hand.

Think of the hands that cut and stitched them, people whose names you'll never know; if no shoes are nearby, rub your palms together slowly instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each stroke.
